newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela signs S.Africa's new liberal abortion law.
newsitem.headline: Mandela signs S.Africa's new liberal abortion law.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela has signed South Africa's new abortion bill, clearing the way for one of the world's toughest abortion laws to be replaced with one of the most liberal, a health official said on Wednesday.
Despite strong protests from opposition parties and anti-abortion groups, the law gives girls of any age the sole right to decide whether to have an abortion.

Doctors and midwives have to advise a child to consult her parents -- but the law specifically states that the abortion will not be denied if the girl refuses to inform her parents. The controversial law sets no age limit, so girls of any age will in future qualify for a legal abortion.
"The Choice on Termination of Pregnancy Bill has been signed by the president. It is now an act of parliament," Department of Health official Eddie Mhlanga said in a statement.

The abortion bill -- the most controversial moral question tackled by South Africa's first democratic parliament -- passed its final legislative hurdle on November 5 when it was approved by 49 votes to 21 in the Senate.

Mhlanga said the health department would only begin to implement the provisions of the new law from February 1, 1997, so that hospitals would be able to cope and to ensure that enough health workers were trained to perform the procedure.

Pointing to medical statistics which show at least 425 women die each year from botched backstreet abortions, Mhlanga said the department would also push ahead with nationwide campaigns to persuade women to use contraception to avoid pregancies.

Mandela must still issue a proclamation to put the new act into operation. Until then, the old abortion law dating back to 1975 are still operational. This allows abortion only in the case of rape, incest or if there is an immediate danger to the mental or physical health of the mother.

Under the new law, women and girls will be entitled to a state-funded abortion on demand during the first 12 weeks of pregnancy if they have no private medical aid schemes, and, subject to widely defined conditions, for a further eight weeks.
